summary:
Botswana decriminalised consensual sexual conduct between adults through its own courts. The High Court struck down Penal Code Section 164(a) and (c) on 11 June 2019 in Letsweletse Motshidiemang v Attorney General, and the Court of Appeal upheld that judgment on 29 November 2021, holding that such laws "incentivise law enforcement agents to become key-hole peepers and intruders into the private space of citizens." The two paragraphs were formally deleted from the statute book in March 2026 by the Rectification of the Laws (Penal Code) Order, 2026. Before that, the offence covered heterosexual and homosexual sodomy alike and carried up to seven years' imprisonment.

Prosecution was rare even while the offence stood. The U.S. State Department's 2011 Human Rights Report recorded that police "did not target same-sex activity" that year and found no reported violence based on sexual orientation or gender identity in 2011. Former President Festus Mogae told the BBC that during his ten years in office he instructed police not to arrest or harass gay people, while declining to change a law he said would cost him an election.

One provision remains unaddressed in the sources. Canada recommended at the 43rd session of the Universal Periodic Review in May 2023 that Botswana repeal Penal Code Section 167, which covers same-sex conduct between women; Botswana did not accept the recommendation, and no source in the inventory records a subsequent repeal of Section 167. Botswana likewise declined a recommendation to introduce an administrative process for legal gender recognition, with the review noting that "a clear administrative process ... was yet to be introduced" (para 570).

Legal gender recognition has nonetheless been won case by case. In September 2017 the High Court held that the Registrar of National Registration's refusal to change a transgender man's gender marker violated his constitutional rights to dignity, privacy, freedom of expression, equal protection, freedom from discrimination and freedom from inhumane and degrading treatment. In December 2017 the same court ordered the government to recognise the gender of transgender woman and activist Tshepo Ricki Kgositau, who received a female identity card after a four-year legal battle and gender confirmation surgery in December 2016; she dedicated the victory to "every single trans diverse person in Botswana." Human Rights Watch records the trans legal-gender right as confirmed across 2017 to 2022. Recognition therefore rests on litigation rather than on a standing administrative route.

The constitutional framework has moved in the same direction. In June 2019 the High Court ruled that "sex" in Section 3 of the Constitution must be "generously and purposively interpreted" to include sexual orientation; legal commentator Carmel Rickard wrote that this gives LGBTQ Batswana "an even stronger, constitutionally-based argument" against discrimination.

Official rhetoric has been openly divided. In February 2011 the Deputy Speaker of the National Assembly said he would have those who practise homosexuality killed if he held the power. President Ian Khama deported the American anti-gay pastor Steven Anderson in September 2016, stating "we don't want hate speech in this country." In November 2018 President Mokgweetsi Masisi acknowledged that people in same-sex relationships "have been violated and have also suffered in silence for fear of being discriminated" and said they deserved protection. Afrobarometer recorded tolerance of a homosexual neighbour rising from 43% in 2016 to 50% in 2021, a level that still leaves roughly half the population unwelcoming.
tangentialFactors:
Botswana's precedent wins have not translated into settled practice. The Southern African Litigation Centre noted on 20 May 2024 that the 2016 Court of Appeal order compelling registration of LEGABIBO, the 2017 High Court order requiring the state to change a trans man's identity documents from female to male, and the 2021 Court of Appeal decriminalisation all stand, yet implementation across Botswana and Namibia "has not been satisfactory so far." The gap between judgments and administrative delivery is therefore documented but not quantified by these sources.

A draft constitutional amendment would add discrimination protection for intersex persons and people with disabilities. In deliberations in June 2024 the Minister of Labour and Home Affairs told legislators to keep "intersex" and "same-sex" as distinct categories, an instruction civic groups read as narrowing the scope of the wider review. Whether the amendment is enacted is unresolved in the sources.

Societal hostility has a documented official edge beyond the courtroom. The 2011 Human Rights Report recorded societal discrimination against LGBT people at the time, and the wider report assessed violence against women, prison conditions and discrimination against the San. LEGABIBO and activists characterised the government's 2019 appeal against decriminalisation as "an affirmation of persistent homophobia and transphobia."
localsOnly:
LEGABIBO is Botswana's principal LGBTIQ+ organisation and a legally registered body, its registration secured by the 2016 Court of Appeal order on freedom of association, expression and assembly. It runs advocacy and awareness campaigns alongside sexual-health and HIV work, including a World AIDS Day 2017 commemoration in Bobonong, and maintains resource strands covering coming out, law and constitution, and help and support.

Legal gender recognition for residents has been obtained through individual constitutional litigation rather than a routine registry procedure, which means a resident seeking a marker change must fund and argue a case. Community infrastructure for that litigation and for peer support exists, but it operates alongside roughly half the population recording no tolerance of a homosexual neighbour as of 2021.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Penal Code Section 167 survived the March 2026 Rectification of the Laws (Penal Code) Order is unresolved: the inventory records only the deletion of paragraphs (a) and (c) of Section 164, and records Canada's 2023 recommendation to repeal Section 167 as not accepted. No source consulted states its current status.

No source in the inventory establishes that an administrative gender-recognition procedure now exists; the 2023 Universal Periodic Review record states it was yet to be introduced, and later material does not revisit the point. Confirmation that the 2017 rulings remain operative in 2026 rests on Human Rights Watch's 2017 to 2022 window rather than on a more recent audit.

The 2011 Human Rights Report is fifteen years old and speaks to police conduct and reported violence at that date; no post-2021 enforcement statistics on police treatment of trans visitors appear in the inventory. The status of the draft constitutional amendment on intersex and disability discrimination is also unresolved, as is the scope of the wider review process that civic groups criticised.
